digest.top_line: HyTEC prostate SBRT: 5-yr TCP 95% at EQD2 90 Gy (36.1 Gy/5 fx) low-intermediate risk vs 102 Gy (38.7 Gy/5 fx) high risk, 4,821 pts.
digest.tldr: Five AAPM HyTEC pooled dose-response models, all study-level, none randomised. Prostate carries the most actionable dose targets: 36.1 Gy/5 fx for 95% TCP in low-intermediate risk, rectal C39Gy ≥40% for late ≥G3 bowel (OR 8.7). Stage I NSCLC maximal LC at PTV-periphery 50±1 Gy/5fx; recurrent previously-irradiated H&N reirradiation suggested at 40 to 50 Gy/5fx.

sites.intro: Liver SBRT GI risk modeled on Rx dose only; pooled series reported no stomach, duodenum or bowel doses.

studies.name: HyTEC Liver SBRT Dose-Volume Effects
studies.tldr: Pooled probit NTCP: G≥2 GI D50 48.0 Gy, G≥3 GI D50 87.1 Gy by Rx dose; no significant liver-enzyme dose response vs MLD (P = .10).
details: 🔍 Pooled study-level review of liver SBRT series in PubMed through May 2014
🔍 Studies were included only if they reported both toxicity and dose-volume data
🔍 Probit NTCP fit by maximum likelihood, using physical dose rather than BED

details.text: 📊 Probit fit parameters by endpoint (95% CI)

details: 📊 Liver enzyme fit (5 studies) was not significant (P = .10), so dose independence can't be excluded
📊 A mean Rx dose of 50 Gy in 3-6 fx kept the modeled G≥3 GI risk below 10%
📊 In series planning with ≥700 cm³ to ≥15 or ≥17 Gy, G≥3 GI was 9.3% (11 of 118), 68% CI 6.6% to 12.8%

details.text: 🔗 QUANTEC MLD limits fall under a 20% probability of G3 enzyme toxicity on this fit
subdetails: Primary liver cancer: 13 Gy (3 fx), 18 Gy (6 fx)

details.text: ⚠️ Grade 5 liver failure was reported in 3 series but not modeled
subdetails: Andolino: 4 of 8 HCC pts with baseline CP ≥8

details: ⚠️ GI risk was modeled on Rx dose because stomach, duodenum and bowel doses weren't reported
⚠️ Primary and metastatic disease were pooled, although mets were reported to tolerate RT better

verdict.rationale: Study-level pooled NTCP from heterogeneous series. Rx dose stands in for GI organ dose, primaries and mets are pooled, and the liver-enzyme fit is nonsignificant.
verdict.audience: Liver SBRT, mostly 3-6 fx, for HCC, IHC or liver metastases

studies.significance: The dose response appeared in GI toxicity, not in liver enzymes. G≥2 GI had a D10 of 18.4 Gy, and a mean Rx of 50 Gy in 3-6 fx kept G≥3 GI under 10%. Because Rx dose stood in for gastric and duodenal dose, central tumors near the hilum (reported to carry higher GI risk) still need organ-specific constraints.
studies.monday_clinic: In HCC or liver mets planned for 3-6 fx SBRT, this supports QUANTEC MLD limits as the liver-enzyme constraint. It does not address liver-function decline in CP ≥8 HCC, where one series saw liver failure in 4 of 8 pts.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: HyTEC **quantitative review** of PubMed liver SBRT series through May 2014, with **study-level** toxicity rates fit to **probit** dose-response models by maximum likelihood. For overlapping reports, only the most recent series with the endpoint was kept. CIs come from profile likelihood and a 2000-sample bootstrap.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Series of **HCC, IHC and liver metastases**, alone or mixed, with Child-Pugh A through C represented. Inclusion required **both toxicity and dose-volume data**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Mostly **3 to 6 fx**; Goodman used single-fraction treatment. Doses were usually prescribed to cover the PTV with the **70% to 85% isodose line**, with motion management and per-fraction image guidance. Modeling used **physical dose, not BED**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Three modeled endpoints: **G≥3 liver enzyme elevation vs MLD**, **G≥2 general GI vs Rx dose** and **G≥3 general GI vs Rx dose**. General GI combined fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, gastritis, ulcers, GI pain and colitis.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: The **liver enzyme fit was not significant (P = .10)**, and the 95% CI for its D50 had no upper bound. Both GI fits were **statistically significant**. Parameters are in the table above.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Child-Pugh decline after SBRT was reported in **10% to 30%** of pts with primary liver cancer. **Grade 5 liver failure** appeared in 3 series and was linked to worse baseline Child-Pugh status, progression of tumor vascular thrombosis and heavy prior systemic therapy.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The review **reaffirms QUANTEC** MLD limits (13 Gy/3 fx and 18 Gy/6 fx for primary disease; 15 Gy/3 fx and 20 Gy/6 fx for mets), placing them under a **20%** modeled G3 enzyme risk. For **liver-function decline** in HCC, it points to Velec's MLD **<18 Gy (6 fx)** instead.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts receiving 3-6 fx liver SBRT for HCC, IHC or liver metastases. Does not represent CP ≥8 HCC, where liver failure rather than enzyme elevation drove the reported grade 5 events.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Son's MLD **included the GTV**, unlike every other series, and Lee's data point may have **skewed** the liver fit. Liver-function decline and liver failure **were not modeled**, and series published after May 2014 are absent.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The useful output is the **GI curve**, which is a prescription-dose proxy and not an organ constraint. On the liver side, the review **reaffirms rather than refines** existing limits. Its more durable contribution may be the proposed **reporting standard** (full absolute DVHs, liver minus GTV, baseline ALBI and Child-Pugh), which would allow future pooling.

studies.interpretation:
This report reduces a decade of heterogeneous single-institution liver SBRT series to three probit curves, and they carry unequal weight. The liver curve is the weakest. With 17 events across 288 pts in five series, the fit could not reject a model with no dose dependence. That does not show that mean liver dose is irrelevant. It shows that grade ≥3 transaminase elevation is a coarse endpoint, that the MLD spread across series is narrow, and that baseline liver function varies enough to swamp a dose signal at this sample size. The endpoint that actually harms cirrhotic pts, Child-Pugh decline and liver failure, was too inconsistently reported to model at all. The grade 5 events the authors describe clustered in pts with worse baseline function, including 4 of 8 with CP ≥8 in one series. A reader should take the liver result as 'no evidence against QUANTEC', not as evidence for it.

The GI curves reached statistical significance, but the x-axis is the prescription dose, not the dose to stomach, duodenum or bowel. That substitution holds only if prescription isodoses and lesion geometry are similar across series, which the authors assume more than demonstrate. Central lesions near the hilum, reported to carry higher GI risk, are exactly where Rx dose and duodenal dose separate. The general GI endpoint also lumps fatigue and nausea with ulceration and colitis. The low G≥2 D10 probably reflects that composite more than mucosal injury, so it should not be read as a constraint for a hollow viscus. The G≥3 D50 has an upper confidence bound near 194 Gy, which reflects sparse events, not tolerance.

Against QUANTEC, this is a confirmation built on overlapping assumptions rather than an independent test. The QUANTEC MLD limits land under a 20% modeled enzyme risk. Series that planned with 700 cm³ spared to 15 or 17 Gy reported G≥3 GI of 9.3%. Huang's HCC cohort under the same 700 cm³ rule still saw G≥2 GI of 28%, a reminder that a liver-sparing rule says little about adjacent bowel. For liver-function decline in HCC, the authors defer to Velec's MLD <18 Gy (6 fx), an admission that the enzyme endpoint is not the one that matters for cirrhotic pts.

Pooling primaries with metastases probably biases the curves in both directions. Pts with mets usually have a larger reserve of healthy liver, so a pooled curve likely overstates their risk and understates the risk in small cirrhotic livers. Using physical dose across single-fraction and 6-fraction schedules adds further noise. Two things could make the GI fits misleading: if the series at higher prescriptions also treated more peripheral lesions, or if a single outlier series drives the slope, as the authors suspect Lee's did for the liver curve.

In practice, nothing here should move a constraint you already use. What it supports is the reporting agenda: absolute DVHs, liver minus GTV, organ doses at small absolute volumes, and baseline and follow-up Child-Pugh and ALBI. Without those, the next pooled analysis will face the same ceiling.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The GI curve, not the liver curve, carries the dose signal. A mean Rx of 50 Gy in 3-6 fx kept G≥3 GI under 10%, but that was modeled on Rx dose, so central lesions near the hilum still need gastric and duodenal constraints. On the liver side, the review reaffirms QUANTEC MLD limits rather than refining them.

open_questions: Toxicity differences between liver mets, HCC and IHC
GI organ-specific dose limits beyond prescription dose
Validated MLD limit for liver-function decline in HCC

sites.intro: Stage I T1-T2 NSCLC dose targets from pooled TCP fits; no model fit well by χ2/ndf, regrowth best.

studies.name: HyTEC Local Control After SBRT for Stage I NSCLC
studies.tldr: Pooled TCP modeling of 46 SBRT series predicts maximal LC at PTV-periphery 43±1 Gy/3fx, 47±1 Gy/4fx, 50±1 Gy/5fx in T1-T2 stage I NSCLC.
details: 🔍 Systematic review: 160 SBRT articles identified (published through May 2014), 46 met quality criteria
🔍 3268 pts treated at ≥6 Gy/fx, plus 211 pts from 3 studies at 3-4 Gy/fx added to fit the shoulder
📊 1, 2, 3 and 5yr TCP for T1, T2 and T1+T2 fit to LQ, USC and regrowth models as a function of BED
📐 None of the three models fit well by χ2/ndf; regrowth gave the best fit
📐 Regrowth α/β approximately 25 Gy (T1), 19 Gy (T2), 21 Gy (T1+T2 combined)

details.text: 📊 Required physical dose (Gy) for maximal TCP by model and stage (PTV dose = PTV covered by 80% isodose line)

details: 🔗 Historic conventional RT (2-3 Gy/fx to ≈54-60 Gy): long-term LC ≈30-70%, OS ≈15-30%
⚠️ Censoring intercurrent deaths may leave a healthier evaluable subset, so 1-3yr actuarial LC may be overestimated
⚠️ LC mostly called radiographically; post-SBRT fibrosis and early FDG uptake can mask or mimic recurrence
⚠️ Most series reported outcomes only up to 3yr; OS collected but not modeled
⚠️ Surgical series count lobar and hilar/mediastinal failure as local failure, so LC vs surgery is not like-for-like

verdict.rationale: Study-level fit across 46 published prospective and retrospective series, not IPD; authors report none of the three TCP models fit the data well.
verdict.audience: Medically inoperable stage I NSCLC (T1-T2, ≤5 cm), SBRT candidates

studies.significance: The usable output is Table 2: maximal LC needs physical dose of 43±1, 47±1 and 50±1 Gy at the PTV periphery (80% isodose) in 3, 4 and 5 fx, with T2 needing more (45±1/50±1/53±1 Gy) than T1 (42±1/46±1/48±1 Gy). That argues for stage-adapted prescription, not de-escalation.
studies.monday_clinic: In medically inoperable peripheral T1-T2 stage I NSCLC, this supports SBRT in 3-5 fx within the modeled PTV-periphery dose band over lower doses; it does not extend to central tumors or tumors >5 cm.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Systematic review with study-level TCP modeling: PubMed search identified **160** SBRT series for stage I NSCLC through May 2014, and **46** met quality criteria (N≥10, dose homogeneity, follow-up, LC reported). Retrospective series were admitted if they met the same criteria.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Medically inoperable stage I NSCLC, T1-T2.** Series with fewer than 10 pts, stage above T2, or lung oligometastases were excluded. Typical selection in included series: FEV1 < 1.2 liters or DLCO < 50%, staged by CT and/or PET-CT, with suspected nodal involvement excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: 3268 pts were treated at **≥6 Gy/fx**, and 3 studies (211 pts) at 3-4 Gy/fx were added to anchor the shoulder of the curve. Described ITV-to-PTV margins were 3-8 mm axial and 5-10 mm cranio-caudal, with CTV = GTV and no margin per ICRU 62.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Local control** (no local progression at the primary on CT or PET-CT) at 1, 2, 3 and 5 yr. OS was collected but **not modeled** because reporting was inconsistent, and distant failure was not recorded.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **No model fit well** by χ2/ndf; regrowth fit best, with α/β approximately **25 Gy (T1), 19 Gy (T2), 21 Gy (combined)**. LQ and USC fits reached nearly the same required doses as regrowth for T1+T2.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Historic conventionally fractionated RT (2-3 Gy/fx to ≈54-60 Gy) gave long-term LC of ≈30-70% and OS of ≈15-30%, and the ablative 3-5 fx regimens modeled here sit on the plateau of the TCP curve. Comparisons with surgery are not like-for-like, because surgical series count lobar and hilar/mediastinal failure as local failure.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents medically inoperable, mostly peripheral T1-T2 stage I NSCLC ≤5 cm treated with 3-5 fx SBRT. Does not represent central tumors, tumors >5 cm, or node-positive disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: In a comorbid cohort, censoring intercurrent deaths likely **inflates 1-3yr actuarial LC**. Radiographic LC calls are confounded by post-SBRT fibrosis and early FDG uptake, and most series stop at 3 yr. The literature window closes in May 2014.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The steep modeled dose-response supports keeping the PTV-periphery dose in the **43-50 Gy band in 3-5 fx** rather than de-escalating, and the model predicts no LC gain above it. T2 tumors need more dose than T1 at every fraction number, which favors stage-adapted prescription.

studies.interpretation:
This pooled analysis matters more for its shape than for any single parameter. Across 46 published series of medically inoperable stage I NSCLC, modeled tumor control rises steeply with physical dose and then flattens, and three structurally different radiobiological models put that shoulder in nearly the same place. For combined T1 and T2 tumors, the regrowth model places the dose for maximal control at 43±1 Gy to the PTV periphery in 3 fractions, and the LQ and USC models at 44±1 Gy. All three agree on 47±1 Gy in 4 fractions and 50±1 Gy in 5. The authors say plainly that none of the models fits well by χ2/ndf. That candor makes the convergence the real finding: when models disagree on mechanics but agree on the dose needed to reach the plateau, the dose recommendation is more credible than any fitted constant behind it.

The fitted α/β ratios, approximately 25 Gy for T1 and 19 Gy for T2 under the regrowth model, are better read as fitting parameters than as tumor biology. They absorb whatever the classical framework fails to capture at ablative dose per fraction. A high α/β also flattens the penalty for spreading dose across more fractions, which fits the modest step in required physical dose from 3 to 5 fractions. In practice, this supports choosing fraction number on proximity to organs at risk rather than on expected control, provided total dose stays in the modeled band.

The stage split is the most actionable detail, and it is easy to miss in the combined headline. Under the regrowth fit, T2 tumors need 45±1 Gy at the PTV in 3 fractions versus 42±1 Gy for T1, and 53±1 versus 48±1 Gy in 5 fractions. If the model is even roughly right, a single prescription for all stage I tumors underdoses larger lesions or overdoses smaller ones. It argues for stage-adapted dosing rather than a uniform schedule.

Several methodological choices should temper confidence, and most push in one direction. The data are study-level, not patient-level, so each series contributes one dose and one control rate despite heterogeneous prescription conventions and dose-calculation methods. That heterogeneity is why the authors' reporting recommendations ask for algorithm, heterogeneity correction and prescription point. Censoring intercurrent deaths in a comorbid population likely inflates actuarial local control, because pts who died with occult progression drop out as controlled. Radiographic assessment through post-SBRT fibrosis and early FDG avidity adds noise in both directions. Most series stop at 3 years. The shoulder is anchored partly by 211 pts from three studies at 3-4 Gy per fraction, inserted because intermediate-dose data were sparse, so the region of the curve that sets the threshold is also the region with the least data.

What the analysis does not settle is just as clear. It is silent on central tumors and on tumors larger than 5 cm, which were underrepresented and carry less favorable outcomes. It cannot support a comparison with resection, because surgical series define local failure more broadly. And with literature closing in May 2014, it predates contemporary motion management and dose-calculation practice. Read correctly, it gives prospective dose-adaptation trials a defensible floor to test against.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Table 2 is the read: maximal LC needs 43±1, 47±1 and 50±1 Gy at the PTV periphery (80% isodose) in 3, 4 and 5 fx, and T2 needs more than T1 at every fraction number (53±1 vs 48±1 Gy in 5 fx). That supports stage-adapted prescription over a uniform or de-escalated schedule.

open_questions: Does stage-adapted dosing (higher for T2) improve LC prospectively?
Optimal SBRT dose for central tumors and tumors >5 cm
True LC once competing-risk censoring is accounted for

sites.intro: Two HyTEC prostate SBRT reviews: TCP dose targets by risk group, and normal-tissue dose-volume thresholds for rectum, bladder, urethra.

studies.name: HyTEC Prostate SBRT Normal Tissue Dose-Toxicity (Heterogeneous-dosing Phase 2)
studies.tldr: Rectal C39Gy ≥40% predicted late ≥G3 bowel toxicity (OR 8.7, AUC 0.83); urethra Dmax ≥47 Gy predicted ≥G2 urinary (OR 4.2) in 4-5 fx SBRT.
details: ⚠️ Source record mismatch: metadata cites Fuller phase 2 (Eur Urol Oncol 2018); full text is Wang et al HyTEC review
🔍 AAPM HyTEC review of prostate SBRT series, PubMed 2001-2018; NTCP refits on four series with dose/volume data

details.text: 📊 Dose thresholds associated with late toxicity, NTCP refits (5-fx physical dose)

details: 📊 Rectum V50Gy model: TD50 5.9cc (5.1-7.1), AUC 0.93
📊 Urethra 20% G2 risk level: D1cc 47 Gy, D0.1cc 49 Gy, Dmax 50 Gy (5 fx)
📊 50 Gy/5 fx escalation: 6 of 61 (10%) CTCAE G3-4 rectal toxicity, 5 needed colostomy
📊 Sunnybrook: RTOG ≥G2 late urinary 5% at 35 Gy vs 48% at 40 Gy

subdetails: Prior TURP: late G2-3 hematuria 21% vs 2%
Prostate > vs ≤ 60 cc: late G2-3 urinary 15% vs 8%
QD vs QOD (Stanford): late G1-2 urinary 56% vs 17%, bowel 44% vs 5%; learning-curve confounded

details: ⚠️ Bladder 17 Gy cutpoint chosen to maximize the OR; optimistic until externally validated
⚠️ Urethral models discriminate poorly: AUC 0.60, 0.62, 0.61 for D1cc, D0.1cc, Dmax

verdict.rationale: Working-group review with NTCP refits of four series; output is planning objectives, and authors state firm dose/volume recommendations cannot be made. No efficacy endpoint.
verdict.audience: Low-intermediate risk prostate cancer, 4-5 fx photon SBRT

studies.significance: Model discrimination splits by organ. Rectal models reached AUC 0.83 (C39Gy) and 0.93 (V50Gy), urethral refits reached only 0.60, 0.62 and 0.61, and the 17 Gy bladder cutpoint was picked to maximize its OR. The rectal high-dose limits are the ones backed by evidence. The urethral and bladder thresholds are planning goals.
studies.monday_clinic: In low-intermediate risk prostate cancer planned for 5-fraction photon SBRT, this supports rectal high-dose limits as the best-grounded planning objective, with urethral and bladder thresholds as softer goals; it does not extend to SBRT boost, salvage after prior RT, or proton plans.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: AAPM working group (HyTEC) review of prostate SBRT series published **2001-2018** via PubMed search, limited to analyses of late urinary, bowel or sexual toxicity/QOL. **Four** series with patient-level dose/volume data were refit with probit or LKB NTCP models.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Mostly **low-intermediate risk** prostate cancer treated with photon SBRT in 5 or fewer fractions. Excluded: series under 40 pts (except sexual outcomes), SBRT boost, proton series, non-English and acute-only reports.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Outside early dose-escalation work, prescriptions were **35-40 Gy in 4-5 fractions**, all with daily image guidance (CyberKnife fiducial tracking, Calypso, or pre-treatment fiducial imaging). The UCSF 4-fraction data were converted to 5-fraction equivalent dose with α/β=3 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Rectal high-dose metrics gave the strongest models (V50Gy AUC **0.93**). The bladder mean-dose association held for **incontinence QOL only**. Obstruction/irritation (p=0.36) and bowel QOL (p=0.40) models were not significant.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: HYPO-RT-PC is cited for similar cancer control and toxicity with a 7-fraction regimen vs conventional fractionation. PACE and NRG-GU005 are named as the ongoing SBRT vs conventional comparisons. The ASTRO/ASCO/AUA guideline advised against doses above **36.25 Gy**, but the authors judge severe toxicity risk low up to **40 Gy**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents low-intermediate risk prostate cancer treated with 4-5 fraction photon SBRT under daily image guidance. Does not represent SBRT boost, salvage after prior RT, or proton therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Few events and **data-driven cutpoints** give wide intervals that will likely shrink on validation. Toxicity scales (RTOG, CTCAE, EPIC, IPSS) and definitions of 'late' varied across series, so the data could not be pooled.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Planning objectives should include at minimum a **Dmax or similar high-dose constraint**, plus a moderate-dose constraint to cover volume effects. Holding **rectum Dmax to the prescription dose** is the main bowel lever. For urinary toxicity, prostate size, baseline symptoms and prior TURP count as much as OAR dose.

studies.interpretation:
This report is most useful as a ranking of which prostate SBRT constraints rest on outcome data and which rest on convention. The authors say plainly that firm tolerance doses cannot be set, and the modeling supports that claim unevenly across organs. The rectal analysis is the strongest part. In the Kim dose-escalation series, circumferential and volumetric high-dose metrics separated pts with severe bowel toxicity from those without (AUC 0.83 for C39Gy, 0.93 for V50Gy), and the clinical anchor is clear: colostomies occurred at the 50 Gy level. That gives a rectal high-dose cap, such as holding rectum Dmax at the prescription dose, the clearest evidence of any constraint here.

The urethral and bladder results deserve more caution than their p-values suggest. Urethral models refit from the UCSF 4-fraction data discriminated barely better than chance (AUC 0.60, 0.62, 0.61). The original authors had found no Dmax association at all, and the Dmax ≥47 Gy signal appeared only after reanalysis and conversion with an assumed α/β of 3 Gy. The bladder mean-dose threshold of 17 Gy was chosen because it maximized the odds ratio, which is the standard recipe for an optimistic estimate, and its interval (1.3-45.0) is wide. Neither threshold should be treated as a tolerance. Both are reasonable planning goals that need external validation in cohorts with prospectively collected DVHs.

The prescription-dose question is where the report speaks most directly to current practice. The ASTRO/ASCO/AUA guideline steered away from doses above 36.25 Gy because of higher grade 1-2 toxicity. The Sunnybrook contrast (5% vs 48% late ≥G2 urinary at 35 vs 40 Gy) supports that caution for mild to moderate effects. Even so, the authors judge grade 3 or higher risk to be low up to 40 Gy, and they argue that OAR dose and prescription isodose line may matter as much as the nominal prescription. That argument targets heterogeneous CyberKnife plans with larger hotspots. It moves the escalation debate away from the prescribed dose and toward what the plan delivers to the urethra and rectal wall.

The non-dosimetric findings carry less weight. The Stanford QD vs QOD contrast is tangled up with an early institutional learning curve. The anticoagulant, TURP and gland-size associations come from single-institution series with uncontrolled selection. Toxicity scales and definitions of late effects varied widely, which is why the authors did not attempt pooling.

What could make these thresholds wrong is mostly motion and delineation. Planned OAR dose at simulation may not match delivered dose once bladder and rectal filling vary. Spacers, MRI-based urethral contouring, and SBRT boost or salvage settings fall outside the data entirely. PACE and NRG-GU005 should supply prospective toxicity data. The authors also ask that every series report at least OAR maximum and D1cc, and that is the practical step that would let these models be tested.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The authors judge severe toxicity risk low up to 40 Gy despite the guideline's 36.25 Gy ceiling, and they weigh OAR dose and prescription isodose line as heavily as the nominal prescription. For heterogeneous CyberKnife plans, urethral hotspot control and a rectal Dmax held at prescription matter more than the prescription number.

open_questions: OAR constraints for SBRT boost or salvage after prior RT
Do spacers or MRI urethral contouring shift these thresholds?
QD vs QOD vs weekly delivery and late toxicity

studies.name: HyTEC Prostate SBRT Tumor Control Probability
studies.tldr: 5-yr TCP 95% at EQD2 90 Gy (36.1 Gy/5 fx) for low-intermediate risk vs 102 Gy (38.7 Gy/5 fx) for high risk; 25 cohorts, 4,821 pts.

details.text: 📊 5-yr FFBR-based TCP dose targets by risk group (α/β=1.5)

details: 🔍 AAPM HyTEC systematic review plus Poisson TCP dose-response model, series published through March 2018

details.text: 🔍 Model fit drew only on cohorts with ≥5 yr f/u

details: 🔍 Regimens 32-50 Gy in 4-5 fx; most prescriptions 35-40 Gy
🔍 All fiducial-guided; 16 cohorts CyberKnife, 7 conventional linac
⚠️ No reviewed cohort below ~80 Gy EQD2: the 71 Gy (90% TCP) low-intermediate point is model extrapolation
⚠️ Prescription dose only; no dose-volume data, so intraprostatic dose not modeled
⚠️ Authors flag the 446 high-risk pts as likely highly selected
🔗 HYPO-RT-PC: 7-fx SBRT-like regimen gave similar 5-yr control and toxicity vs conventional fractionation

verdict.rationale: Ecological dose-response fit across pooled single-arm cohorts at prescription dose only, without dose-volume data; the high-risk curve rests on 3 studies, 85 pts.
verdict.audience: Localized prostate cancer, mostly low/intermediate risk (NCCN/D'Amico)

studies.significance: The low-intermediate 90% TCP point (EQD2 71 Gy, 31.7 Gy/5 fx) sits below the ~80 Gy floor of every reviewed cohort, so it is extrapolation, not a de-escalation floor. The data-supported read is 95% TCP at 36.1 Gy/5 fx; the high-risk 38.7 Gy/5 fx target rests on 85 pts.
studies.monday_clinic: In low- and intermediate-risk localized prostate cancer planned for 5-fraction SBRT, this supports the 35-40 Gy prescription range on biochemical control grounds; it does not set a dose for high-risk disease or address SBRT as a boost to IMRT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: AAPM HyTEC (WGSBRT) **systematic review** of PubMed series through March 2018, with a **Poisson TCP dose-response model** fitted to cohorts with ≥5 yr follow-up. **25 cohorts, 4,821 pts**: 2 registries (RSSR 437, RPCR 1743), 3 multi-institutional, the rest single-institution.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Definitive SBRT monotherapy (≥6 Gy/fx, ≤5 fx) for localized prostate cancer; series with <40 pts, protons, and non-English reports excluded. Risk mix when reported: **low 2,235, intermediate 1,894, high 446**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **32-50 Gy in 4-5 fx**, most prescriptions 35-40 Gy; BED (α/β=1.5) 183.1-383.3 Gy. All fiducial-based IGRT, 16 cohorts on CyberKnife and 7 on conventional linac.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **FFBR** by Phoenix nadir+2 in all but 3 cohorts, 5-yr values used whenever possible, stratified by NCCN or D'Amico risk group.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Low-intermediate curve fitted on **9 studies (1069 pts)**, high-risk curve on **3 studies (85 pts)**. Dose targets by risk group are in the detail table.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Randomized dose-escalation trials set **≥75.6 Gy** conventional EBRT as standard, and nine randomized trials support moderate hypofractionation. HYPO-RT-PC found a 7-fx SBRT-like regimen gave similar 5-yr control and toxicity to conventional fractionation; this model is consistent with that, not a randomized test of it.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents low- and intermediate-risk localized prostate cancer treated with fiducial-guided 4-5 fx SBRT monotherapy. Does not represent high-risk disease with confidence, proton SBRT, or SBRT as a boost to IMRT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Target delineation, **PTV margin and seminal vesicle coverage varied** by institution and are folded into the dose term. Three cohorts used non-Phoenix failure definitions, and every EQD2 value hinges on the **α/β=1.5** assumption.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: For low-intermediate risk, 5-fx prescriptions in common use sit high on the modeled TCP curve, with **95% TCP at 36.1 Gy/5 fx**. High-risk dose, durability beyond 5 yr, and SBRT as a boost to IMRT remain open.

studies.interpretation:
This paper is best read as a map of where the prostate SBRT literature sits, not as a dose prescription. Every cohort it pooled was single-arm, and the dose-response curve is fitted across institutions rather than within them. The slope therefore carries whatever else differed between those centers: platform, PTV margin, seminal vesicle coverage, ADT use and length of follow-up. That makes the model ecological, and a dose-response that emerges from it is a hypothesis about dose rather than a measurement of it.

Within that frame, the low-intermediate risk result is the most defensible. The 95% TCP estimate of 36.1 Gy in 5 fractions sits inside the 35-40 Gy band most series prescribed, so it interpolates through dense data. The 90% estimate is a different kind of number. The authors state that no reviewed cohort had an equivalent dose below approximately 80 Gy, and the 71 Gy EQD2 point falls in the faded, extrapolated part of their own curve. Treating 31.7 Gy in 5 fractions as an acceptable de-escalation floor would take the model somewhere its authors explicitly said not to go.

The high-risk estimates deserve less weight still. That curve rests on 3 studies and 85 patients with 5-year follow-up, drawn from 446 high-risk patients overall whom the authors themselves describe as likely highly selected. The 37.6 and 38.7 Gy figures are better read as a direction (high-risk disease appears to need more dose for the same biochemical control) than as a target. Whether extra dose is best spent on the prostate, the seminal vesicles or elective nodes is a question this dataset cannot answer, because it reports prescription dose only.

Two technical choices shape every number. The EQD2 conversion assumed an α/β of 1.5, so the EQD2 values shift if that assumption is wrong, while the physical 5-fraction doses are what a reader actually prescribes. And with most cohorts treated on CyberKnife, delivered intraprostatic dose likely departs from the prescription in ways that vary by institution, which the model cannot see without dose-volume data. The endpoint is also softer than local control: FFBR by Phoenix, with 3 cohorts using other failure definitions and no biopsy-based assessment of the gland.

Against the randomized evidence, the model is consistent rather than discordant. Dose-escalation trials established conventional EBRT of at least 75.6 Gy, moderate hypofractionation has nine randomized trials behind it, and HYPO-RT-PC found a 7-fraction regimen comparable to conventional fractionation at 5 years. PACE-B has since tested SBRT against longer schedules in a randomized design. What this paper adds is a cross-cohort sense that the 5-fraction schedules in common use sit high on the TCP curve for low-intermediate risk disease. It does not settle optimal high-risk dose, durability beyond 5 years, or SBRT as a boost to IMRT, and the authors flag all three as open.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The low-intermediate 90% TCP point (EQD2 71 Gy, 31.7 Gy/5 fx) lies below the ~80 Gy floor of every reviewed cohort, so it is extrapolation, not a floor for de-escalation. The data-supported read is 95% TCP at 36.1 Gy/5 fx; the high-risk 38.7 Gy/5 fx target rests on 85 pts.

studies.tldr: 3-yr LC 15% at 26.8 Gy vs 40% at 44.4 Gy (5-fx equivalent); 40 to 50 Gy/5fx suggested for SBRT reirradiation of recurrent previously-irradiated H&N.

🔍 293 articles screened, 25 candidates, 16 not fully evaluable; 8 used for the dose-response model

verdict.rationale: Pooled retrospective series with study-level dose averaging. The dose-response may reflect selection (better-prognosis pts dosed higher). LC definitions are heterogeneous. No prospective dose comparison.
verdict.audience: Unresectable recurrent previously-irradiated H&N cancer, SBRT >6 wk after prior RT

studies.significance: Dose matters for how long control lasts, not for the 1-yr response: the 1-yr LC dose-response did not reach significance (P=.096), while the 2- and 3-yr models reached P<.01. Volume gates the prescription. Below 25 cm3 the response flattens above 45 Gy/5fx, so escalating to 45 to 50 Gy is a question for larger recurrences, weighed against carotid blowout rates of up to 10% to 20%.
studies.monday_clinic: In an unresectable in-field recurrence after prior conventional RT, this supports higher over lower SBRT reirradiation doses scaled to tumor volume. It does not extend to SBRT as a boost within 6 weeks of primary RT, primary SBRT, or benign tumors.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: AAPM working group **systematic review with pooled logistic dose-response modeling**. 8 publications and >300 cases were included. 1-, 2- and 3-yr LC and 1- and 2-yr OS came from each report, digitized from KM curves when the time points were not stated.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Locally recurrent, **previously irradiated malignant H&N** treated with SBRT **more than 6 weeks** after primary RT. Benign tumors were excluded, and the source studies selected unresectable recurrences. HPV status was not available for most studies.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Mostly CyberKnife with thermoplastic masks. Contemporary series used **GTV-to-PTV expansions of 2 to 6 mm**. All doses were normalized to a **5-fraction equivalent** with the Withers LQ formulation at α/β 10 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** local control and overall survival. Local control here means local or locoregional failure, as each source study defined it.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Dose-response was significant for **2- and 3-yr LC (P<.01)**, not for 1-yr LC or 2-yr OS. The model estimates are in the table above.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: The authors cite a prior phase 1 dose-escalation study and a phase 2 with concurrent systemic therapy in support of the dose range. Other institutions report **fatal complications in up to 10% to 20%**, mainly carotid blowout, even at lower doses.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Surgical salvage remains the standard. The authors describe conventional reirradiation with or without chemotherapy as limited by toxicity and suboptimal outcomes. Rwigema 2011 first showed that larger tumors need higher dose for equivalent 1-yr locoregional control, and this pool extends that across 8 series.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents unresectable, locally recurrent, previously irradiated malignant H&N treated with SBRT more than 6 weeks after primary RT. Does not represent SBRT as a planned boost, primary SBRT, or benign tumors.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Doses are **planned, not delivered**, and each study's dose is a weighted average weighted by initial N, not by pts at risk. Target coverage, prescription isodose and tumor volume are **outside the model**. Few pts remain at 2 and 3 yrs, which is where the significant fits sit.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The steeper slopes at later time points suggest escalation buys **durability of control** more than early response. Whether dose causes better survival or follows it cannot be separated here, and the cetuximab and fractionation-schedule effects remain unquantified.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this pooled model is less in any single estimate than in giving a heterogeneous literature a common dose axis. SBRT reirradiation for recurrent head and neck cancer grew institution by institution, with single-fraction radiosurgery, five-fraction CyberKnife courses and six-fraction schedules reported side by side, which made it nearly impossible to say whether one center's prescription was more aggressive than another's. Collapsing everything to a 5-fraction equivalent at α/β 10 Gy is crude, and the authors admit it, but it turns a scattered set of case series into something a planner can reason about.

The pattern of the results deserves more attention than the headline range. At 1 year, the model cannot tell a 25.6 Gy course from a 40.7 Gy course with confidence (P=.096). The signal only appears at 2 and 3 years. One reading is that early response is driven by tumor bulk and biology, and higher dose mainly delays the regrowth that eventually claims most of these pts. That fits the clinical experience that reirradiated tumors often shrink and then come back. If that reading is right, the case for escalation is strongest in pts expected to live long enough to benefit from durability, which is the same group most exposed to late vascular and soft-tissue toxicity.

The main threat to a causal reading is selection, and the authors name it. Fitter pts with smaller, more favorable recurrences were plausibly offered higher doses, and survival-linked factors such as HPV status, reirradiation interval and concurrent cetuximab were not modeled. The 2-yr OS trend (model P=.060) points the same way as LC, which is what you would expect whether dose drives survival or survival prognosis drives dose. A single series contributing a third of the cases also anchors the late-time-point fits, so the 2- and 3-yr curves are partly one institution's experience re-expressed.

The volume-stratified suggestion is the most usable output, and it comes from the earlier Rwigema dose-volume data more than from the pooled model, which excludes volume. A flat response above 45 Gy/5fx for tumors under 25 cm3 argues against routine escalation in small recurrences. Escalation into the 45 to 50 Gy range is a hypothesis for bulky disease, not an established gain.

Against all this sits the toxicity record. Fatal carotid events reported at up to 10% to 20% in some series, including at modest doses, mean the dose-response for control cannot be read alone. The companion NTCP work and the observation that every-other-day schedules lower carotid risk belong in the same planning decision. The paper settles the direction (sub-30 Gy schemes look inadequate for durable control) but not the ceiling, and a prospective dose-comparison or volume-stratified trial is what would test whether the modeled gain survives randomization.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Dose matters for how long control lasts, not for the 1-yr response: 1-yr LC dose-response P=.096, while the 2- and 3-yr models reached P<.01. Below 25 cm3 the response flattens above 45 Gy/5fx, so escalating to 45 to 50 Gy is a question only for larger recurrences, weighed against fatal carotid events of up to 10% to 20%.
